Chronology 6 — David, Solomon, and the Portrayal of God's Chosen

This chapter isolates a systematic pattern, not a single episode: the two texts portray God's chosen servants on opposite philosophies.

The Bible's text

  • David: adultery with Bathsheba and the engineered death of Uriah (2 Sam 11), exposed and rebuked (2 Sam 12), penitential Ps 51.
  • Solomon: in old age his foreign wives turn his heart; he builds high places for other gods (1 Kings 11).
  • The pattern is general: patriarchs, prophets, and kings are shown "warts and all" — deceit, violence, idolatry, doubt.

The Qur'an's text

  • Dawud and Sulayman are righteous prophets. The Bathsheba/ Uriah episode is absent; Q 38:21–25 (the two disputants) has Dawud seek forgiveness, but no adultery or murder is narrated.
  • Sulayman is "an excellent servant" (Q 38:30); his alleged idolatry is not affirmed (Q 2:102 transfers blame to devils, not Solomon).
  • General doctrine: *prophetic impeccability ('isma)* — prophets are divinely protected from grave sin.

Collision

This is the clearest "different by design" divergence in the dossier:

BibleQur'an
Portrayal of the chosenflawed, sinning humansmorally elevated, protected
David's adultery/murdernarrated and condemnednot narrated
Solomon's idolatrynarrateddenied/deflected
Governing doctrinegrace despite sin'isma (impeccability)

Logic — and why it matters methodologically

  • The Bible's embarrassing detail engages the criterion of embarrassment: in historiography (and in mainstream historical-Jesus scholarship), a tradition that damages its own heroes is less likely to be invented and is weighed as a mark of authenticity. This is a recognized neutral-historian tool, not a Christian apologetic invention.
  • 'isma is a theological axiom about what befits a prophet — it is not a historical claim and is not falsifiable as such.
  • Both are internally coherent. But they are *different kinds of claim*: one invites historical assessment; the other states a doctrine.

Arbiter verdict — the chosen

Present. Bible: fallible servants saved by grace. Qur'an: protected servants befitting revelation.

Weigh.

  • Methodological weight, Bible: the criterion of embarrassment is a standard, neutral historiographic tool and favours the non-invention of the unflattering accounts.
  • Theological axiom, Qur'an: 'isma is coherent as doctrine but contributes no historical evidence; it explains the divergence rather than evidencing it.
  • Symmetry check: this is not a corruption proof against either — it is a difference of portrayal philosophy.

Judge. On historical-evidentiary value of the narratives: advantage Bible — by the very neutral criterion historians apply, its self-damaging detail is harder to dismiss as invention. On internal theological fittingness: the Qur'an's elevated prophetology is coherent on its own terms. Whether revelation should embarrass its heroes (authenticity) or protect them (fittingness) is, once more, the non-arbitrable value premise. This is the dossier's tidiest example of "different by design, not by corruption."
